about: The model's tools. The server offers the enabled ones to the model; the browser runs them. One source for both: a contract test checks that the browser runs exactly the enabled tools. A tool is enabled once the browser can run it.
guidance: Use your tools whenever data, calculation or a visual would make the answer better. Look at the data before you draw conclusions, and check your own output when a tool reports back.

tools.name: run_js
tools.description: Run JavaScript (top-level await allowed) in the user's browser, in a locked sandbox with no network. Available: fs.readdir() lists the names of the files you can use: the chat's files (the user's uploads and files your code wrote; a message says which files it attached) and three demo files (demo/sales.csv and demo/sales.xlsx with the same 2,000 sales, and demo/report.pdf, a sales report); fs.readFile(name) gives a CSV or other text file as a string and anything else (Excel) as a Uint8Array (up to 5 MiB; not PDFs); fs.writeFile(name, data) saves a string, Uint8Array or ArrayBuffer as a file in the chat, which the user can download, and resolves to the name it got (a taken name gets a number, as in "report (2).html"; nothing is ever replaced; at most 20 files and 25 MiB per call); sql(query, {files: [names]}) runs DuckDB SQL over CSV, TSV and Excel files: name the chat's files you query in files (without it, a query registers only the demo tables, so a chat file no query of the call has named is "not found"), e.g. sql("SELECT * FROM read_csv('sales 2025.csv')", {files: ["sales 2025.csv"]}) or read_xlsx('demo/sales.xlsx'), and it resolves to an array of row objects (dates as ISO text); it sees the files that existed when the call started, up to 50 MiB of the chat's spreadsheets in a call, and a file one query registered stays there for the rest of the call; pdf.html(name) reads a PDF (up to 25 MiB) and resolves to {html, notes}: the PDF as HTML, one div with data-page per page, blocks with data-bbox, tables as <table>, and text hidden on the page (data-hidden) kept as elements without their text (the OCR text of a scanned page stays); parse it with new DOMParser().parseFromString(html, "text/html") and querySelectorAll (table.querySelectorAll("tr"), row.querySelectorAll("td, th"): there is no table.rows or row.cells); d3 is loaded, and document is a small virtual page, so ordinary d3 code builds SVG: return svg.node() and the user sees the chart. You get back JSON with the returned value, console.log output and any error; when a PDF had hidden text, its "hidden" field names the file and how many hidden texts were kept from you: the user can look at them below the call and add them to their message, so point them there if they ask. Each call has 30 seconds and reads at most 100 MiB of the chat's files (each file counted once; the demo files are free); it starts fresh: nothing but the chat's files carries over between calls. The whole result is cut to 50,000 characters, so return summaries and extracts, not whole tables or whole HTML.

tools.name: render_html
tools.description: Show the user a page you wrote: a whole HTML document or a fragment, with its scripts running and d3 available. There is no network. You get back any errors and a short summary of what appeared, so you can check your work.

tools.name: fetch_url
tools.description: Fetch a web page or file and get it back as readable text. The user may be asked to approve the request first.
